ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Avoiding misleading routine imaging

A 9-month-old has a typical first episode of bronchiolitis with diffuse findings and no focal signs. A trainee proposes a routine chest radiograph to decide whether antibiotics are needed. What is the best reason to avoid that approach?

  1. Nonspecific changes may be mistaken for bacterial pneumonia
  2. A radiograph reliably determines whether RSV or another virus is present
  3. Radiographic severity reliably determines the required antibiotic dose
  4. An abnormal radiograph reliably establishes bacterial coinfection
  5. A normal radiograph safely overrides clinical respiratory distress
Answer and explanation

Nonspecific changes may be mistaken for bacterial pneumonia

Routine imaging rarely changes typical bronchiolitis management and nonspecific abnormalities can prompt inappropriate treatment.

Option explanations

Nonspecific changes may be mistaken for bacterial pneumonia: Routine imaging rarely changes typical bronchiolitis management and nonspecific abnormalities can prompt inappropriate treatment.

A radiograph reliably determines whether RSV or another virus is present: Radiographs do not identify the specific respiratory virus.

Radiographic severity reliably determines the required antibiotic dose: Antibiotics are not routine bronchiolitis treatment, and radiographic appearances do not set a dose.

An abnormal radiograph reliably establishes bacterial coinfection: Atelectasis and other bronchiolitis changes may mimic pneumonia without bacterial coinfection.

A normal radiograph safely overrides clinical respiratory distress: Clinical severity still determines care even if radiography is normal.
